title: Sign-OPT: A Query-Efficient Hard-label Adversarial Attack
authors: Minhao Cheng, Simranjit Singh, Patrick Chen, Pin-Yu Chen, Sijia Liu, Cho-Jui Hsieh

pages.title: You only need the sign
pages.subtitle: The Sign-OPT idea in one sentence

blocks.html: OPT made the hard-label attack a real optimization problem, but every gradient step was expensive because estimating the boundary distance $g(\theta)$ required a full binary search, repeated many times. Sign-OPT's insight is that to take a good descent step you do not need the value of the directional derivative at all — you only need its sign, and the sign can be obtained with a single extra query per probe direction.

We remain in the hard-label / decision-based world: the attacker queries the model and observes only the final predicted label — no probabilities, no gradients — and is judged by queries-to-success, the number of queries to reach a small perturbation norm.
Sign-OPT inherits OPT's reformulation. We still search for a direction $\theta$ that minimizes the distance to the boundary, where that distance is

Read: $g(\theta)$ is how far you must travel along $\theta$ before the label flips, and we want the direction that makes that distance smallest. Everything that follows is about estimating the gradient of $g$ more cheaply than OPT did.

pages.title: Why OPT's gradient estimate is wasteful
pages.subtitle: Magnitude is expensive; direction is cheap

blocks.html: OPT estimates the directional derivative by computing $g(\theta + \beta u)$ and comparing to $g(\theta)$. But $g$ is defined by a boundary crossing, so each value needs a binary search — many queries — just to learn a single number. Most of that precision is then thrown away the moment you take a normalized descent step.
The key observation: whether $g$ increased or decreased when you nudged $\theta$ by $u$ can be decided without finding the new boundary distance. You only have to check one point.

pages.title: One query tells you the sign
pages.subtitle: The single-query directional test

blocks.html: Take the current boundary radius $g(\theta)$. Now look at the perturbed direction $\theta + \beta u$ and evaluate the classifier at that same radius. If the point is now adversarial, then the boundary along $\theta + \beta u$ is nearer than along $\theta$, so $g$ decreased; if it is still correctly classified, the boundary moved farther and $g$ increased. That is exactly the sign of the directional derivative — from a single query.

blocks.tex: \text{sign}\big(g(\theta + \beta u) - g(\theta)\big) \;=\; \begin{cases} -1 & \text{if } f\!\left(x_0 + g(\theta)\,\tfrac{\theta+\beta u}{\lVert\theta+\beta u\rVert}\right) \neq y_0 \\ +1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}

blocks.html: Read plainly: probe at the old radius but in the slightly rotated direction; one hard-label query says "already across the boundary" (sign $-1$, this rotation helps) or "not yet" (sign $+1$, this rotation hurts).

pages.title: Building a gradient from many signs
pages.subtitle: The Sign-OPT estimator

blocks.html: Average the sign outcomes over many random probe directions $u_q$ to assemble an estimated gradient, then descend on $\theta$. Each random direction costs just one query (plus the one shared binary search to know $g(\theta)$ for the current $\theta$), so a whole gradient estimate is dramatically cheaper than OPT's.

Read: each random direction $u_q$ votes with $\pm 1$ depending on whether rotating toward it brings the boundary closer; the weighted sum points, on average, toward directions of smaller boundary distance. It is a biased estimator (signs discard magnitude) but the authors show it is good enough to descend, and overwhelmingly cheaper.
Trading exact gradient magnitudes for one-bit sign votes is the whole game: a little bias in the direction, an enormous saving in queries.

pages.title: An order of magnitude fewer queries
pages.subtitle: Sign-OPT versus OPT and Boundary Attack

blocks.html: On MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet, Sign-OPT reaches a given perturbation norm with roughly 5–10× fewer queries than OPT, and far fewer than the Boundary Attack, often producing smaller final perturbations at the same query budget. The improvement compounds because cheaper gradient estimates mean more descent steps per query budget.

The authors also give convergence analysis for the sign-based estimator, showing that despite using only one bit per direction the iteration still converges to a stationary point of $g$. The method works for untargeted and targeted attacks and needs nothing beyond the label oracle.

Sign-OPT showed that the query cost of hard-label attacks could be cut by an order of magnitude with a single conceptual move — replace expensive distance estimates with cheap sign tests. That pushed label-only attacks from "possible but impractical" toward "a realistic threat against deployed APIs."

It sits between OPT (which it accelerates) and HopSkipJump (a contemporaneous line that estimates the gradient direction directly at the boundary using Monte-Carlo sampling and adds geometric step sizing). Together they define the modern frontier of query-efficient hard-label attacks.
Sign-OPT: you only need the sign of the directional derivative, obtainable with one extra query per probe direction — yielding far fewer queries than OPT for the same attack.
